repositories.name: SynthID Remover
repositories.description: Regenerate pixels to break invisible AI watermarks

paragraphs: Upload an image you generated yourself and get back a PNG with no metadata and a regenerated pixel layer. A before and after slider shows what changed.

SynthID is Google DeepMind's watermark for AI-generated images, audio, text and video. It is built into the pixels and is invisible to people (source). OpenAI's verifier checks for it, and that page is the only checker this Space was tested against.

The C2PA, EXIF and XMP metadata disappear because the output is a fresh PNG. The invisible watermark lives in the pixels, so the pixels are redrawn. The app encodes the image, noises it part of the way, and denoises it again with Qwen-Image-2.1.
features: Subtle (default) redraws the image at 17 steps, lines the redraw up halfway with your original, then takes only the 16 to 32 px luma band from it. Every other pixel and all the color stay yours, so faces and structure…
Strong returns the full redraw after 17 steps. It removed the mark on each of three images, but it rewrites the image, including faces.

paragraphs: OffGridSchedula turns a pasted chat (or a flyer screenshot) into calendar events, catches conflicts, and drafts the reply — right from your phone, no app, no account, no setup. iOS allows neither background iMessage access nor a persistent on-device LLM server, so there's no autonomous on-device agent to install; instead, a foreground Shortcut (docs/automations.md) hands a thread or screenshot to the agent in two taps (optionally using a remote model via INFERENCEBASEURL).

The model runs on your own server or even on the phone itself and not on a cloud AI service. Your chats aren't shipped off to a third-party AI to be read; agent reads your snippet in memory and discards it after replying. The run trace you can optionally share is a redacted, sent to the agent you control that turns it into ready-to-add calendar events.
Hardware-aware. With under-powered hardware, the app warns users with an upgrade banner rather than hanging, the real model needs a tiny GPU.

paragraphs: Interactive demo of polygen applied to the visual tokens that a vision-language model consumes. Upload an image, type a question, and compare the un-spliced Qwen2-VL baseline against the polygen + LoRA path side by side.
The recipe transfers across four public benchmarks (ScienceQA, MMMU, VQAv2, DocVQA) on Qwen2-VL-2B and Qwen2-VL-7B.

A vision-language model takes an image through a vision encoder, then a "merger" that down-samples the patch grid, and finally feeds the resulting visual tokens into the LLM alongside the text prompt. For Qwen2-VL on natural-image VQA the visual-token count is in the low hundreds; for document images it climbs into the thousands. The LLM forward pass attends across all of those visual tokens at every generation step.
features: Attention compute. The LLM's attention is quadratic in sequence length, so shrinking the visual prefix reduces attention-layer FLOPs by 1 - (Lcompressed / Lbaseline)^2. At the demo's operating point a typical photo goes…
Storage. Multimodal corpora are typically dominated by raw images. Storing the compressed merger representation instead cuts storage materially: about 5.1x at T=3 and 7.5x at T=2.
Multi-LoRA per-tier could lift the last 0.5-1pp at fixed T.
Moving the polygen encode onto the accelerator could convert the attention-FLOP reduction into end-to-end wall-clock savings on single-shot inference.
Large cumulative-context workloads (multi-page documents, video, multi-image) are where the quadratic attention reduction would compound, and are a natural next measurement target.

These aren't templates you fill in manually; they're systems that do the work.

paragraphs: An animated, self-contained walkthrough — built to present at conferences — of what happens when you vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct-FP8 --model-impl transformers using the Transformers modeling backend. It follows the control flow from the CLI, through backend-class resolution and the MRO, into Base.init rebuilding the model, and then sends a batch through — watching execution hop back and forth across the vLLM ⇄ Transformers boundary at the attention and MoE seams.

Qwen3-VL-FP8 (a multimodal, FP8-quantized MoE) is used because it exercises more of the backend than a plain text model: the multimodal path (TransformersMultiModalMoEForCausalLM + vision tower + M-RoPE), FP8 quantization through SupportsQuant, pipeline-parallel deletions (the Base.init walk-through is shown at PP=2), the fuser system (QKV / RMSNorm / MoE), and the fact that a native vLLM implementation exists, so the backend must be explicitly requested.

repositories.name: FontMap
repositories.description: Google Fonts mapped by visual similarity

paragraphs: An interactive map of 1,465 Google Fonts organized by visual similarity, using FontCLIP embeddings blended with Google Fonts style tags and measured proportions, laid out with t-SNE.
Inspired by IDEO's Font Map (2017, Kevin Ho), a different take on the same idea, fully open source.
Full demo video (52 s) · Typographic trailer (19 s) — source in trailer/ · Experiments (size by use, who drew the fonts you know) — source in src/experiments/
features: Visual similarity map - fonts that look alike are physically close together

1,465 Google Fonts - full catalog; fonts that ship the same Latin glyphs (e.g. Noto script variants, Battambang = Roboto Slab) and Playwrite "Guides" variants are folded into one point and stay searchable by name
Your own text - type any sample text and it follows you as you move from font to font
Any glyph - type a letter, digit or & on desktop to redraw the whole map with that character (?glyph= keeps it in the URL)
Keyboard navigation - arrow keys step to the nearest neighbour in that direction

whatItDoes.text: An interactive map of 1,465 Google Fonts organized by visual similarity, using FontCLIP embeddings blended with Google Fonts style tags and measured proportions, laid out with t-SNE.
